_comment: Dogmas-and-doctrine levels 19-21: real debate vs. real heresy, moral theology, applying moral theology to a hard case

questions.prompt: The previous level named the real debate between congruism and Bañezianism over how grace and free will cooperate. How did the Church actually resolve this specific real dispute?
choices: Paul V ended the Congregatio de Auxiliis in 1607 without condemning either school
The Church formally condemned both schools as heretical
The Church declared one school the only permissible Catholic position, condemning the other as heresy
The debate was never actually addressed by any real Church authority
questions.correctAnswer: Paul V ended the Congregatio de Auxiliis in 1607 without condemning either school
questions.explanation: This is a real, precise historical fact worth knowing directly -- after years of real investigation, the Holy See closed this specific debate without declaring either side heretical, permitting Catholics to hold either real position in good conscience.
questions.hint: Recall the previous level's own real mention of a decree that ended this specific investigation.

citations.reference: Paul V, decree ending the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1607)

questions.prompt: True or False: The fact that the Church left the congruism-Bañezianism debate formally open means both positions must actually be true at once.
questions.explanation: False, and this is a real, careful distinction -- leaving a real question open means the Church has not determined which explanation is correct, not that contradictory explanations are somehow both simultaneously true.
questions.hint: Consider the real difference between 'the Church has not decided' and 'both sides are correct.'

questions.prompt: What real line actually separates a permitted theological debate, like congruism versus Bañezianism, from a real heresy, like the Pelagianism this app's own Heresies topic covers?
choices: A permitted debate explains how a settled dogma works; a heresy denies or distorts the dogma itself
There is no real difference at all -- both are simply matters of theological opinion
A permitted debate is decided by majority vote among living theologians, while heresy is decided by seniority
A permitted debate always involves fewer real participants than a heresy does
questions.correctAnswer: A permitted debate explains how a settled dogma works; a heresy denies or distorts the dogma itself
questions.explanation: This is the real, precise line -- congruists and Bañezians both fully affirm that grace is real, necessary, and freely given, and that human freedom is real and genuinely cooperates; they differ only on how to explain that real cooperation. Pelagianism, by contrast, actually denied grace's real necessity.
questions.hint: Recall Pelagianism, covered in this app's own Heresies topic, and consider exactly what it denied that congruism and Bañezianism both still affirm.

questions.prompt: True or False: Both congruism and Bañezianism fully affirm the Second Council of Orange's own real condemnation of semi-Pelagianism -- neither school actually denies grace's real necessity.
questions.explanation: True, and this is exactly why both schools remain within orthodoxy -- they share the same real, settled starting point (grace is truly necessary, truly gratuitous, and human freedom truly cooperates), differing only in how they explain the mechanism of that real cooperation.
questions.hint: Recall the Second Council of Orange, covered a few levels back in this topic and directly in this app's own Heresies topic.

questions.prompt: Why does it actually matter, practically, that a Catholic can tell the difference between a real permitted debate and a real heresy?
choices: Without it, a Catholic would wrongly call open questions heresy, or wrongly call heresy an open question
Because it has no real practical bearing on anything -- the distinction is purely academic
Because it means a Catholic never actually needs to think carefully about any theological claim at all
Because it proves the Church has, in fact, never really settled any doctrinal question
questions.correctAnswer: Without it, a Catholic would wrongly call open questions heresy, or wrongly call heresy an open question
questions.explanation: This real distinction protects against two opposite real mistakes -- an unwarranted rigidity that brands every open question heresy, and an unwarranted looseness that treats every real heresy as just another legitimate opinion.
questions.hint: Consider the two opposite real mistakes a Catholic could make without this level's own real distinction in hand.

citations.reference: Paul V, decree ending the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1607)

questions.prompt: True or False: This level's own real distinction -- debate about mechanism versus denial of dogma -- is the same real distinction this app's own Heresies topic used when it distinguished Jansenism from ordinary Catholic teaching on grace.
questions.explanation: True. Jansenism was judged heresy not because it discussed grace at all, but because it actually distorted the dogma itself (denying real, universal sufficient grace); congruism and Bañezianism, by contrast, both leave that dogma fully intact.
questions.hint: Recall Jansenism, covered in this app's own Heresies topic, and consider what it actually denied versus what congruism and Bañezianism both still affirm.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about real theological debate and real heresy to what it actually means.

pairs.right: Ended a real investigation without condemning either congruism or Bañezianism
Different explanations of how an already-settled dogma actually works
Denies or distorts the settled dogma itself, not merely its mechanism
Protects against both unwarranted rigidity and unwarranted looseness

questions.explanation: These four facts together give a real, precise tool for telling a genuinely open theological question apart from a real, settled heresy -- exactly the tool this level's own real point requires.
questions.hint: Two rows describe the real historical case; two describe the general real principle it illustrates.

citations.reference: Paul V, decree ending the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1607)

questions.prompt: True or False: Having now covered how to tell real debate from real heresy, this topic's next level turns to Catholic moral theology -- conscience, the natural law, and Veritatis Splendor.
questions.explanation: True. Having named the real line between open debate and settled dogma, this topic's next level turns to a genuinely different real area, moral theology, where a similar real precision about conscience and the natural law becomes essential.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: What real, general habit has this level now added to the real precision this topic has practiced since its levels on ex opere operato and Trinitarian vocabulary?
choices: Distinguishing what a real dogma actually settles from what it genuinely leaves open for further real theological explanation
Assuming every theological question the Church has not yet condemned must therefore already be a settled dogma
Assuming every theological debate the Church has not yet resolved must therefore be a real heresy
Avoiding any real engagement with open theological questions altogether
questions.correctAnswer: Distinguishing what a real dogma actually settles from what it genuinely leaves open for further real theological explanation
questions.explanation: This level's own real habit -- reading a dogma's real, precise boundary to see exactly what it settles and what it leaves open -- extends the same careful method this topic has practiced since its earliest levels on precise vocabulary.
questions.hint: Consider what this level's own real distinction has actually trained a careful reader to check before calling something heresy.

questions.prompt: Given this level's picture of real debate versus real heresy, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: Catholic moral theology -- conscience, the natural law, and Veritatis Splendor
A complete repeat of this same level's material about real theological debate
A jump backward to material this topic already fully covered several levels earlier
A subject entirely unrelated to anything this topic has covered so far
questions.correctAnswer: Catholic moral theology -- conscience, the natural law, and Veritatis Splendor
questions.explanation: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers -- moving from doctrinal precision about grace to moral theology's own real precision about conscience, the natural law, and how a person actually judges right from wrong.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

citations.reference: Paul V, decree ending the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1607)

questions.prompt: Veritatis Splendor teaches that the moral quality of an act depends on three sources together: the object chosen, the intention behind it, and the circumstances. If someone gives money to the poor (a good object) specifically in order to be seen and praised (a bad intention), what is the act's actual moral quality?
choices: The act is not good overall -- a bad intention can corrupt an act whose object is otherwise good, since all three sources (object, intention, circumstances) must be good together for the act itself to be good
The act is fully good, since giving to the poor is always good regardless of intention
Intention is irrelevant to morality; only the object chosen ever matters
The act is morally neutral, since good and bad elements simply cancel out
questions.correctAnswer: The act is not good overall -- a bad intention can corrupt an act whose object is otherwise good, since all three sources (object, intention, circumstances) must be good together for the act itself to be good
questions.explanation: This is the settled framework Veritatis Splendor teaches, not one option among several: a good intention cannot redeem an intrinsically evil object, but neither can a good object alone guarantee a good act if the intention is corrupt -- all three sources must be rightly ordered together.
questions.hint: A good object alone doesn't settle the question -- ask what all three sources need to be, together.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 74-78 (1993)

questions.prompt: Proportionalism argues that an act's rightness can be judged by weighing its good and bad consequences against each other, so that even lying could be justified if it produces a greater good (e.g., lying to save a life). What is the Church's actual, SETTLED teaching on this theory, per Veritatis Splendor?
choices: Proportionalism is a rejected error, not a legitimate parallel school of Catholic moral theology -- some acts (including direct lies) are intrinsically evil by their object and cannot be justified by any calculation of consequences, however proportionate the reasoning seems
Proportionalism is a fully approved, legitimate Catholic school, on equal footing with the traditional object/intention/circumstances framework
The Church has never addressed proportionalism at all
Proportionalism is correct specifically in emergency situations, though not in ordinary ones
questions.correctAnswer: Proportionalism is a rejected error, not a legitimate parallel school of Catholic moral theology -- some acts (including direct lies) are intrinsically evil by their object and cannot be justified by any calculation of consequences, however proportionate the reasoning seems
questions.explanation: This is worth being precise about, since it's the level's highest-risk point: unlike level 8's congruism-versus-Bañezianism (a live, Church-permitted internal debate), proportionalism is not held open by the Magisterium as one legitimate school among others. Veritatis Splendor names and rejects it directly, holding that certain acts remain wrong regardless of how favorable the calculated balance of consequences appears.
questions.hint: This is not a live debate the way grace's mechanics were in the previous level -- the Church has actually settled this one.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 75-77 (1993)

questions.prompt: A person acts on a conscience that is sincerely, but wrongly, mistaken -- through no fault of their own (invincible ignorance) -- versus a person whose conscience is wrong because they culpably avoided knowing better (vincible ignorance). How does the Church's teaching on moral responsibility differ between these two cases?
choices: Invincible ignorance can excuse a person from personal guilt for the wrong act, since they could not have known better through no fault of their own; vincible ignorance does not excuse in the same way, since the person bears some responsibility for the ignorance itself
Both cases are treated identically -- ignorance of any kind always fully excuses moral responsibility
Neither case ever excuses moral responsibility under any circumstances
Vincible ignorance excuses fully, while invincible ignorance never does
questions.correctAnswer: Invincible ignorance can excuse a person from personal guilt for the wrong act, since they could not have known better through no fault of their own; vincible ignorance does not excuse in the same way, since the person bears some responsibility for the ignorance itself
questions.explanation: This distinction matters because it keeps two true things together: an objectively wrong act remains objectively wrong regardless of the agent's sincerity, while personal culpability for that wrongness can still be reduced or removed depending on whether the agent's ignorance was avoidable.
questions.hint: Ask whether the person COULD have known better if they had tried -- that's the difference between the two kinds of ignorance.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 62-64 (1993)

questions.prompt: True or false: 'fundamental option' theory -- the idea that a person's basic, deep orientation toward or away from God is what really determines mortal sin, largely independent of individual serious acts -- is affirmed by Veritatis Splendor as compatible with, and even clarifying, traditional Catholic teaching on mortal sin.
questions.explanation: Veritatis Splendor explicitly rejects using fundamental option theory to sever a person's deep orientation from concrete, freely chosen acts -- a grave act, freely and knowingly chosen with full consent, is itself capable of altering a person's fundamental orientation, not something the 'fundamental option' can be quarantined from. This connects directly back to the mortal/venial sin distinction already taught at the Last Things level.
questions.hint: The theory tries to separate deep orientation from concrete individual acts -- the encyclical specifically will not allow that separation.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 65-70 (1993)

questions.prompt: Veritatis Splendor grounds conscience's judgments in the natural law -- a moral order genuinely knowable by human reason, prior to and independent of any specifically revealed command. What follows from conscience being answerable to natural law, rather than conscience simply generating truth on its own?
choices: Conscience is the faculty that discerns and applies an objective moral order it did not invent -- so a conscience can genuinely err about that order, and being sincere does not by itself make a conscience's judgment correct
Conscience creates moral truth freely, and no judgment of conscience can ever be mistaken
Natural law only applies to baptized Christians, not to all human beings
Conscience and natural law are entirely unrelated to one another
questions.correctAnswer: Conscience is the faculty that discerns and applies an objective moral order it did not invent -- so a conscience can genuinely err about that order, and being sincere does not by itself make a conscience's judgment correct
questions.explanation: This is the load-bearing point underneath the whole level: if conscience answers to a real, discoverable order (the natural law), then sincerity and correctness are two different things, which is exactly what makes the invincible/vincible ignorance distinction meaningful in the first place.
questions.hint: If conscience is discerning something real rather than inventing it, sincerity alone can't guarantee it got the answer right.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 40-53 (1993)

questions.prompt: Veritatis Splendor teaches that certain acts are wrong 'always and per se, in other words, on account of their very ______, and quite apart from the ulterior intentions of the one acting and the circumstances' -- the technical basis for calling an act intrinsically evil.
questions.explanation: This is the encyclical's own precise language (n. 80) for what 'intrinsically evil' actually means: the wrongness attaches to the object of the act itself, prior to and regardless of whatever good intention or mitigating circumstance might surround it -- the exact principle proportionalism, rejected in this same level, denies.
questions.hint: This is the first of the three sources of morality named earlier in this level.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 80 (1993)

questions.prompt: A pastor must decide, in a genuinely hard case, how best to walk with someone in an irregular situation toward eventual full conformity with Church teaching -- a real question of pastoral prudence. How does this kind of question differ from the proportionalism question this level already settled?
choices: The moral principle itself (e.g., that a given act remains objectively wrong) is settled and not up for renegotiation; the pastoral question is instead about the prudential, practical path of accompanying a real person toward it -- a different kind of question from whether the principle is true at all
There is no real difference -- both are equally open questions the Church has left undecided
Pastoral prudence means the underlying moral principle changes case by case
Pastoral questions are always doctrinal questions in disguise
questions.correctAnswer: The moral principle itself (e.g., that a given act remains objectively wrong) is settled and not up for renegotiation; the pastoral question is instead about the prudential, practical path of accompanying a real person toward it -- a different kind of question from whether the principle is true at all
questions.explanation: This is the distinction this level is built to keep sharp: a settled doctrinal principle (like the rejection of proportionalism) is not the same kind of question as a genuinely open pastoral-prudential judgment about how best to accompany a particular person in a particular circumstance. Blurring the two -- treating pastoral flexibility as if it renegotiated the principle -- is exactly the mistake to avoid.
questions.hint: Ask whether the TRUTH of the principle is in question, or just the best PRACTICAL way to walk someone toward living it.

questions.prompt: Someone argues: 'if circumstances and intention both matter to an act's morality, then nothing is ever wrong in itself -- it all just depends on the situation.' Where does this argument go wrong, per this level's whole framework?
choices: It ignores that the OBJECT of an act is itself one of the three sources, and that some objects are wrong regardless of intention or circumstance -- circumstances and intention can make an otherwise good act bad, but they cannot make an intrinsically evil object good
It is entirely correct -- morality really does reduce to circumstances alone
Intention and circumstances are irrelevant to morality and should be ignored entirely
The Church has no teaching on how object, intention, and circumstances relate to one another
questions.correctAnswer: It ignores that the OBJECT of an act is itself one of the three sources, and that some objects are wrong regardless of intention or circumstance -- circumstances and intention can make an otherwise good act bad, but they cannot make an intrinsically evil object good
questions.explanation: This is a common one-directional misreading of the three-sources framework: circumstances and intention genuinely affect an act's morality, but that influence only runs one way for intrinsically evil objects -- they can never redeem what is wrong by its object, only ever further corrupt or (for otherwise-neutral acts) shape what would otherwise be acceptable.
questions.hint: Ask whether the three sources work symmetrically in both directions, or only in one direction for certain acts.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 81 (1993)

questions.prompt: Match each moral-theology claim to its status in Catholic teaching.

pairs.left: Proportionalism (consequences alone can justify any act)
pairs.right: Settled error, rejected by Veritatis Splendor

pairs.left: Fundamental option theory (deep orientation independent of concrete acts)
pairs.right: Settled error, rejected by Veritatis Splendor

pairs.left: Congruism vs. Bañezian premotion (how grace and will cooperate)
How best to pastorally accompany someone toward a settled moral truth
pairs.right: Genuinely open prudential question, not a doctrinal one

questions.explanation: Not every disputed-sounding question in Catholic moral and doctrinal theology has the same status -- some are genuinely settled and rejected, some are genuinely still open between legitimate schools, and some are practical questions about applying a settled truth, not about the truth itself. Confusing these categories is the single most common error a well-meaning explainer makes.
questions.hint: Ask, for each item, whether the Church has actually closed the question, left it open between schools, or left open only how to apply it pastorally.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 65-77 (1993)

questions.prompt: Why did Veritatis Splendor need to be written at all -- what was actually at stake, given that the Church had always taught object, intention, and circumstances mattered to morality?
choices: Some Catholic moral theologians had begun using the three-sources language itself to argue for proportionalist conclusions -- using the Church's own traditional vocabulary to smuggle in a rejected calculus of consequences -- so the encyclical had to state precisely what the traditional framework does and does not permit
The Church had never before addressed the relationship between object, intention, and circumstances
The encyclical was written to introduce an entirely new moral framework replacing the traditional one
Nothing was actually at stake; the encyclical merely repeated settled teaching with no new occasion
questions.correctAnswer: Some Catholic moral theologians had begun using the three-sources language itself to argue for proportionalist conclusions -- using the Church's own traditional vocabulary to smuggle in a rejected calculus of consequences -- so the encyclical had to state precisely what the traditional framework does and does not permit
questions.explanation: This is worth knowing precisely because it shows why this level's distinctions matter in practice: proportionalism did not present itself as a rival framework from outside the tradition -- it was argued for using the Church's own traditional terms, redefined at the edges. Veritatis Splendor's task was precision against exactly that kind of internal redefinition, the same pattern Heresies (level 8) named in modern errors that restate old claims in respectable-sounding new language.
questions.hint: The error this encyclical answers didn't come from outside the tradition -- it came from redefining the tradition's own words.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor, n. 4-5, 75 (1993)

questions.prompt: A pastor must decide how best to walk with someone in a genuinely difficult, irregular life situation toward eventual full conformity with Church teaching. Which two real things does the previous level's own moral theology require holding together here?
choices: A real, unchanging norm, and real pastoral patience respecting where a person actually is on that path
Only the objective moral norm, with no real regard for a person's actual circumstances
Only pastoral accompaniment, with the objective moral norm treated as negotiable case by case
Neither -- pastoral situations like this have no real connection to moral theology at all
questions.correctAnswer: A real, unchanging norm, and real pastoral patience respecting where a person actually is on that path
questions.explanation: Veritatis Splendor's own real teaching holds both together -- the objective norm does not bend, but real pastoral care patiently accompanies a person's actual, gradual journey toward living it fully, rather than either abandoning the norm or abandoning the person.
questions.hint: Recall the previous level's own real teaching on intrinsically evil acts, and consider what pastoral care adds without changing that real norm.

questions.prompt: True or False: Real pastoral patience with someone's gradual progress toward a moral norm means the norm itself is only provisionally true, subject to change case by case.
questions.explanation: False, and this is exactly the real error called the 'law of gradualness' turned into 'gradualness of the law' -- real pastoral patience concerns a real person's own gradual journey toward a fixed goal, never the goal itself becoming negotiable.
questions.hint: Consider the real difference between a person growing gradually toward a fixed goal, and the goal itself gradually changing.

questions.prompt: A parish volunteer, applying this level's own real distinction, is asked: 'Doesn't real compassion for someone in a hard situation require softening what the Church actually teaches?' What is the real, careful answer?
choices: No -- real compassion means patient accompaniment on the real path, not pretending the destination changed
Yes -- real compassion always requires changing the objective norm to fit the person's own situation
No -- because real compassion and moral teaching have no real connection to each other at all
Yes -- but only because objective moral norms were never actually real to begin with
questions.correctAnswer: No -- real compassion means patient accompaniment on the real path, not pretending the destination changed
questions.explanation: This is the real, careful answer this level's own distinction makes possible -- compassion and truth are not actually in tension; real compassion is expressed through how a person is patiently accompanied, not by relocating the real destination itself.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own earlier real distinction between a fixed goal and a person's own gradual journey toward it.

questions.prompt: True or False: This level's own real distinction -- fixed norm, gradual journey -- is actually just a restatement of the proportionalism the previous level already rejected.
questions.explanation: False, and this is a real, important distinction to keep straight -- proportionalism claimed the norm itself could be outweighed by good intentions or circumstances; this level's real teaching never touches the norm at all, only how a real person's own journey toward it is pastorally accompanied.
questions.hint: Recall proportionalism, covered in the previous level, and consider whether it changed the norm or only the pace of a person's journey toward it.

questions.prompt: Why does getting this real distinction right actually matter for how the Church engages people in genuinely hard, real situations?
choices: Losing either side produces a real failure -- rigid judgment with no accompaniment, or compassion with no real truth to walk toward
Because it has no real practical bearing on how the Church actually engages anyone in a hard situation
Because it proves objective moral norms are, in the end, actually negotiable after all
Because it means pastoral care should never involve any real, honest conversation about Church teaching at all
questions.correctAnswer: Losing either side produces a real failure -- rigid judgment with no accompaniment, or compassion with no real truth to walk toward
questions.explanation: This level's own real stakes are practical, not abstract -- losing the fixed norm produces a compassion with nothing real to walk toward; losing the real patience produces a rigid judgment with no real accompaniment. Both real failures are genuinely possible, and both are genuinely avoided by holding this level's own distinction rightly.
questions.hint: Consider what actually goes wrong, practically, if either half of this level's own real distinction is dropped.

questions.prompt: True or False: This level's own real method -- holding a fixed truth together with real patience toward a person's own actual journey -- echoes the same real balance this app's own Heresies topic traced between Pelagianism and Jansenism.
questions.explanation: True. Just as the Church refused to collapse grace and freedom into either extreme, she refuses here to collapse truth and real pastoral patience into either extreme -- the same real method, applied to a genuinely hard, lived situation rather than an abstract doctrinal question.
questions.hint: Recall Pelagianism and Jansenism, covered in this app's own Heresies topic, and the real balance the Church held between them.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about applying moral theology to a genuinely hard case to what it actually means.

pairs.right: Never becomes negotiable, whatever a person's own real circumstances
Patiently respects where a person actually is on the real path toward that norm
The real error of treating the goal itself, not just the journey, as gradually changing
Rigid judgment with no accompaniment, or compassion detached from any real truth

questions.explanation: These four facts together show exactly how this level's own real distinction actually plays out in a genuinely hard, lived pastoral situation, not merely as an abstract theological rule.
questions.hint: Two rows name the two real things this level holds together; two name the real errors that result from losing either one.

questions.prompt: True or False: Having now applied moral theology to a genuinely hard real case, this topic's next level turns to the Trinity, divinization, and why the whole of doctrine coheres as one real story.
questions.explanation: True. Having worked through real moral precision down to its own hardest, most concrete pastoral cases, this topic's next level steps back to its own widest possible view -- how everything this topic has covered actually fits together as one coherent story.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: What real, general habit has this level now demonstrated by applying the previous level's own moral theology to an actual hard case?
choices: Precise doctrine is meant to guide real, hard situations, without collapsing into rigidity or compromise
Precise doctrine has no real, practical application to any actual lived situation
Real pastoral care should simply ignore precise doctrine whenever a situation becomes difficult
Real moral theology becomes irrelevant the moment a situation becomes genuinely hard
questions.correctAnswer: Precise doctrine is meant to guide real, hard situations, without collapsing into rigidity or compromise
questions.explanation: This level's own real demonstration -- taking the previous level's moral theology and applying it to an actual hard case -- shows exactly why this whole topic's own real precision has mattered throughout: not for its own sake, but to actually guide real, lived situations faithfully.
questions.hint: Consider what this level actually did with the previous level's own moral theology.

questions.prompt: Given this level's picture of doctrine actually guiding a genuinely hard real case, what does the next level in this topic turn to?
choices: The Trinity, divinization, and why the whole of doctrine coheres as one real story
A complete repeat of this same level's material about applying moral theology to a hard case
A jump backward to material this topic already fully covered several levels earlier
A subject entirely unrelated to anything this topic has covered so far
questions.correctAnswer: The Trinity, divinization, and why the whole of doctrine coheres as one real story
questions.explanation: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers -- stepping back from this level's own concrete, hard case to this topic's widest possible view, showing how everything covered so far actually forms one coherent, real story.
